extractor.note: Partial pass over §§ 5, 8 and 45, the sections in which the reduction and the epochê carry argumentative weight.

coverage_note: Covers § 5 (the insertion of the ego cogito in the universal phenomenological horizon), § 8 (the essence of the phenomenon as the task of phenomenology) and § 45 (the dissimulation and forgetting of the originary essence of revelation). §§ 3 and 7 and the remaining sections carrying hits are not covered.

units.claim: The reduction necessarily precedes the systematic exploration of the transcendental field and makes possible the understanding of absolute consciousness in its ontological signification.
units.quote: The phenomenological reduction necessarily precedes the systematic exploration of the transcendental field. It anticipates, by rendering it possible, the understanding of absolute consciousness in its ontological signification.

units.primary_locator: Cartesian Meditations § 15; Epilogue to Ideen I
units.claim: The transcendental experience the epochê leads to remains subordinated to the conditions of evidence and intuitive realization, hence to the horizon of being in general.
units.quote: The internal "transcendental" and phenomenological experience to which the *epochê* leads thus remains subordinated to the conditions of evidence and of intuitive realization — that is, in fact, to the transcendental horizon of being in general.

units.claim: The transcendentally-reduced pure ego, like empirical consciousness, requires a horizon of presence as the condition of possibility of its own manifestation.
units.quote: the transcendentally-reduced pure ego implies, as condition of possibility of its manifestation — and consequently of every systematic elucidation of its own life — a horizon of presence

units.claim: Appearance is what cannot be refused and what escapes reduction, and a truly positive science is possible only by constant reference to it.
units.quote: What appears is what one cannot refuse, what escapes reduction.

units.claim: The reduction does not sort contents into the certain and the suspended; what it releases as irreducible foundation is the universal essence of every phenomenon as such.
units.quote: The phenomenological reduction does not seek to save certain contents considered as "certain" while others would be struck or suspended.

units.claim: Taken in an ultimate sense the phenomenological reduction and the eidetic reduction are one and the same.
units.quote: For this reason, the phenomenological reduction is one with the eidetic reduction understood in an ultimate sense.

units.claim: The reduction liberates the essence that could not be reduced and alone subsists as condition, and thereby introduces into the sphere of the absolute.
units.quote: The reduction is the liberation of the essence which could not be reduced and which alone subsists, as condition. The reduction then introduces us into the sphere of the absolute.

units.claim: The epochê is the epochê of the world as such, bracketing exteriority itself and the movement of intentionality toward it, rather than obeying the teleology of thought.
units.quote: the ἐποχή is the ἐποχή *of the world*, its bracketing (*mise hors circuit*) — and that with the radical signification of concerning *this world as such*, exteriority itself and the movement toward it of intentionality

units.claim: Because the reduction does not let its origin appear in thought as a motive, it appears to the phenomenologist without foundation and is called unmotivated.
units.quote: the reduction — because it does not let appear its origin in thought and as a *"motive"* — appears henceforth without foundation; it is, according to the famous word of Fink, *"unmotivated."*
